summary: Adds an Extended Administrative Group sub-TLV to the IGP traffic engineering extensions, giving more link colors than the existing limit of 32.

plainLanguage.summary: Links can be given color tags so routes can pick or avoid them. There were only 32 colors. This allows many more.

questions: mpls te link colors more than 32
what is an extended administrative group
how many link colors does mpls te support
what is the eag sub-tlv type for ospf and is-is
how do ag and eag coexist
subtitle: A new sub-TLV that lets MPLS-TE links carry far more than 32 colors.

tldr.problem: MPLS-TE advertises link colors (administrative groups) as a fixed 32-bit bitmask, and large networks can run out of the 32 values quickly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7308 adds an Extended Administrative Group sub-TLV to the OSPF and IS-IS TE extensions. It carries a bitmask of any non-zero length that is a multiple of 4 bytes.
tldr.outcome: Operators can use hundreds or thousands of colors within a single domain, while the first 32 bits stay compatible with the old Administrative Group.

today: RFC 7308 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why 32 Colors Are Not Enough
sections.content:
MPLS Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) lets operators tag links with administrative groups, often called colors or link colors. The existing Administrative Group (AG) is a fixed-length 32-bit bitmask, so a link can carry at most 32 distinct colors. The idea comes from Section 6.2 of RFC 2702, which calls them Resource Classes.

The RFC gives an example. One operator gives each metro region its own bit, such as Seattle, San Francisco, Dallas, Chicago and St. Louis, and then builds tunnels that include or exclude regions. With 32 bits, only 32 metro areas can be represented cleanly. Reusing a bit for different places is described as fraught with peril, and it makes it impossible to build a path that avoids Seattle while including Prague if both share one value.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only have 32 sticker colors for a whole country full of towns, you have to reuse colors and get mixed up. More colors means no mix-ups.

sections.title: Scope and Limits
sections.content:
The number of EAGs has no fixed limit. It is constrained only by protocol-specific restrictions such as Link State Advertisement (LSA) or MTU size, which should still allow hundreds or thousands of bit values.

The intended use case is a single domain. The document provides no way to signal an EAG: there is no analog to the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object of RFC 3209 or the LSP Attributes object of PCEP in RFC 5440. Because of that, constraints expressed with EAGs can only be applied at the ingress.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra colors are used inside one network, and only the router where a trip starts uses them to choose the route.

sections.title: The Extended Administrative Group Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The Extended Administrative Group (EAG) sub-TLV has the same format for OSPF and IS-IS. It is a series of 32-bit Extended Admin Group words. The Type is 26 for OSPF and 14 for IS-IS. The Length is the size of the EAG value in bytes.

The EAG may be any non-zero length, but it MUST be a multiple of 4 bytes. The only limits are protocol-specific or media-specific, such as maximum packet length. The sub-TLV is optional, and it is used in addition to the Administrative Group when an operator wants more than 32 colors.

Numbering follows the old convention: bits 0 (least significant) to 31 (most significant) are the AG. Additional bytes continue the numbering, so the least significant bit of the fifth byte of an 8-byte EAG is bit 32.
sections.plainLanguage: The new tag is a long strip of on/off switches, always added in groups of 32. Switch numbers just keep counting up past 31.

sections.title: Coexisting with the Old Administrative Group
sections.content:
A node that advertises an EAG MAY also advertise an AG. If it advertises both, the first 32 bits of the EAG MUST be identical to the AG. A receiver that has both MUST use the AG for bits 0 to 31 and the EAG for bit 32 and higher. If the AG differs from the first 32 bits of the EAG, the receiver SHOULD report the mismatch to the operator.

This lets nodes without EAG support still learn some color information, and allows an eventual migration away from AG.

A second question is what to do when a node wants a color that a link does not advertise. The RFC says an implementation SHOULD treat desired but unadvertised EAG bits as set to 0. For example, a node that wants links with the 127th bit set will skip a link advertising only 64 EAG bits. An implementation that chooses another strategy SHOULD make the recommended behavior configurable.
sections.plainLanguage: Old routers still read the first 32 switches, so they are not left out. If a switch is missing, you assume it is off.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC states that this extension adds no new security considerations.

IANA is asked to register the sub-TLV in both protocols. For OSPF it goes in the "Types for sub-TLVs of TE Link TLV (Value 2)" subregistry, with value 26. For IS-IS it goes in the "Sub-TLVs for TLV 22, 141, and 222" subregistry, with value 14, marked 'y' for those TLVs like the Administrative Group sub-TLV. The sub-TLV is named "Extended Administrative Group".
sections.plainLanguage: It does not create new safety worries, and the new tag got its own official ID number in the shared lists.

fields.name: Extended Admin Group
fields.desc: First 32-bit word; bits 0-31, matching the AG if both are advertised.
Further 32-bit words, repeated as needed; numbering continues from bit 32.

fields.name: Extended Admin Group
fields.desc: Last 32-bit word. Total length must be a multiple of 4 bytes.
